newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Senate head sees at least 10 states in EMU.
newsitem.headline: French Senate head sees at least 10 states in EMU.

text.p: The European Union is likely to make "a few arrangements" to allow 10 to 12 countries to join the single currency at the start in 1999, the head of the French Senate, the upper house of parliament, says.
In an interview with Reuters, Rene Monory said that not all members of the EU would strictly respect all criteria in the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union.
"When you look at the situation, I am not sure that in 1998 everyone will be ready exactly. There will be problems with debt and with budget deficits," he said.

But it would be regrettable to forego the launch of the euro with 10 to 12 countries "if a (country's deficit) is within 0.2 or 0.3 percent of three percent (of gross domestic product) if the trend is right," he said.
He noted that the Maastricht Treaty allowed for such an interpretation.

"I am convinced that there will be a few arrangements at the last minute round the table. I do not say there will be a lot. It is not being lax, but I would prefer for there to be a little bit of accommodation and have more countries in than be rigid and have only two or three," he said.

"For this currency to have any sense, we must start with at least 10 countries," he said, citing Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, France, Spain, Portugal, Austria, Finland, Ireland, and Italy on condition it continued its efforts at budgetary consolidation.
With a narrower membership, France and Germany would be trapped by those countries left out of EMU which might then be tempted by competitive devaluations.
He also said an acceleration in growth should allow France to meet Maastricht Treaty criteria without additional austerity.
Monory is a member of the centrist UDF party, junior partners in the outgoing RPR-UFF centre-right coalition.

The opposition Socialist party, campaigning for a parliamentary election in May 25/June 1, has called for a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty and says it wants Italy, Spain and Portugal in from the start.
